Frets jumped to ~0.99 across the board, the green→orange gradient **flattened**, and loss halved (0.13 → 0.063). Strum is unchanged (~0.99 recall, p95 ~25 ms — same source, as expected). So the fret gain is purely from the cleaner structure. **Your legato hypothesis was right: the held-across-gaps label was the fret-accuracy ceiling.** And it cleared 0.99 *despite* the ~5-sample y=311 timing handicap — strong signal.

## But detector-fb is a probe, not the deployable label

Here's the catch the probe also reveals: **detector frets are at the wrong time for deployment.** Detector-`pressed` (y=311) leads the photo dip by ~20 ms and *releases when the gem leaves y=311* — which is ~220 ms **before** the strum. A model trained on it would press the fret early and **release it before strumming**. The probe proves clean *structure* is learnable; it doesn't give correct *timing*. (This is exactly the spatial-mismatch the actuator labels were built to dissolve.)

## So the deployable fix: make marvin's *actuator* output clean-structured

We want clean per-note structure **at strike-line timing** — which is what marvin's pipeline already produces, minus the legato hold. That's the [line-263](firmware/marvin/default/src/actuator/timing_pipeline.c#L263) change: stop suppressing the release between separate notes. Then `actuator-fb` labels get clean structure *and* correct timing → expect ~0.99 frets that are actually deployable. Re-capture, retrain.

I'd do it **gated**: suppress the release only if the next same-fret note is within ~X ms (genuinely back-to-back — keeps Expert robustness), release otherwise. On hard mode even an ungated removal would be safe, but gated is the no-regret version.

Let me log the confirmation, and then — want me to implement the gated line-263 change? It's small and localized in `timing_pipeline.c`. You'd reflash marvin (fretboard unchanged this time), re-capture slowride-hard, and we export `actuator-fb` and confirm frets hit ~0.99 with correct timing.

## Strum duration — quick correction

It's **25 ms**, not 40: `TP_STRUM_PULSE_MS = 25u` at [timing_pipeline.c:23](firmware/marvin/default/src/actuator/timing_pipeline.c#L23) (the comment says it mirrors the fret-tuner Python defaults — maybe that's where 40 ms lived historically). It matches what we measured in the captures earlier: strum pulses ran ~5–9 ticks (≈21–37 ms), centered on 6 ticks = 25 ms. If there's another 40 ms constant somewhere I haven't seen, point me at it.

## Your framing is right — and half of it is already baked in

"Rising edge matters most, falling edge/duration much less, going long is fine, no 0-glitches" — that's exactly the right gameplay model, and it maps cleanly onto how we should score and deploy strum:

**Already aligned:** our strum eval is **event/rising-edge based** — `strum_event_timing` matches 0→1 transitions within a tolerance and reports recall/precision/onset-timing. It does *not* grade per-tick duration. So "the rising edge is what counts" is already how we judge it. (The per-tick BCE *loss* still cares about every tick, but the *metric* we trust doesn't.)

**What we're not yet measuring — and should:** the *shape* of the model's predicted strum. The raw thresholded output can do three bad things you're pointing at:
1. **Glitch** (1→0→1 inside one pulse) → the game registers **two** strums → overstrum/break. This is the dangerous one.
2. **Too short** (1–2 ticks) → might not register at all.
3. **Merged** (one long predicted pulse spanning two real strums) → a missed note.

I can add a "capture/analyze" pass to the eval that reports, on the model's predicted strum stream: pulse-duration histogram, glitch count (brief 0-dropouts inside a pulse), count below a min-register threshold, and merged-pulse count. That directly quantifies your concern and tells us whether the raw output is gameplay-safe.

## The robust fix: a deploy-time strum monostable

The clean way to *make* "only the rising edge matters" true is a tiny state machine on the model's output at inference — a retriggerable one-shot:
- On a rising edge (strum prob crosses threshold) → **assert strum for a fixed N ticks** (say 8–10 ≈ 33–42 ms, ≥ marvin's 25 ms with margin), ignoring the model's own falling edge and any glitches during the hold.
- **Refractory period** (~M ticks) before another trigger → prevents double-fire/overstrum.

This *guarantees* no glitches, adequate duration, and "a little long is fine" — by construction. The model then only has to nail the **onset**, which is the part it's good at (recall ~99%). And it's a natural on-device runtime component (cheap, no FPU). I can also apply it in eval to measure how much it cleans up precision and kills glitches versus the raw output.

(Training-side, we *could* also asymmetrically dilate the strum label's trailing edge so "going long" isn't penalized — but the monostable makes that largely moot, so I'd hold off.)

Want me to implement (1) the glitch/duration analysis in the eval metrics, and (2) a parameterized strum monostable applied in eval (hold N, refractory M)? Both are host-side, no re-capture — and the monostable is reusable as the deployment post-processor. We can run them against your current `slowride-hard` model output to see the strum shape immediately.

All green — 21 edge-ai tests pass (4 new for the monostable + pulse stats). Run it with the post-processor on, against the clean-fret `detfb` capture so you see the whole picture:

```sh
cd tools/edge-ai
uv run edge-ai train --overfit ../marvin-perf/captures/slowride-hard-detfb.csv \
    --channels 64 --epochs 60 --tol 15 --window 96 \
    --strum-hold 8 --strum-refractory 4
```

Each epoch now prints two strum lines:
- `raw  …` — the model's predicted strum: event recall/precision/timing **+ pulse shape** (`pulses=… median=…ms glitches=… too_short=…`).
- `mono …` — after the monostable (rising-edge → hold 8 ticks ≈ 33 ms, then 4-tick refractory): same metrics, post-processed.

**What to look for:**
- In `raw`, the **`glitches`** and **`too_short`** counts — that's the thing you flagged: 1→0→1 dropouts and stubby pulses that'd mis-register. I suspect there are a fair number, and they're exactly what's tanking raw precision (~0.6).
- In `mono`, **precision should jump** (glitches absorbed, extra blips merged by the refractory), **recall should stay ~0.99**, **p95 onset timing unchanged** (the monostable preserves the rising edge), and pulses become uniform (`glitches=0`, all 8 ticks). If that's what happens, you're right — the strum was basically fine and just needed clean shaping.

**One knob to watch:** hold + refractory = 12 ticks ≈ **50 ms minimum spacing between strums**. If `mono` recall *drops* below raw, two real strums are landing closer than 50 ms and the refractory is merging them — lower `--strum-refractory` (try 2) or `--strum-hold` (6 = 25 ms, matching marvin). On hard mode that's unlikely, but the numbers will tell us.

This is all uncommitted (metrics + monostable + the 4 tests) — I'll fold it into a commit once we see the numbers, so the message can record whether the monostable actually closed the strum gap. Paste the last few epochs.

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-8 2026-06-04 02:46:32Z)**_

Committed `02d1bb2`. Now the actual problem and the re-run.

## Why it over-fires

This is the **hot `pos_weight=17.3`** (auto-set to the inverse strum frequency). It makes the loss punish *missing* a strum ~17× harder than a *false* one, so the model learns to assert strum very liberally — recall ~0.99, precision ~0.6. The raw stream is also **ragged**: those `glitches=42, too_short=181` are the model stuttering around each real strum, which (with my old buggy monostable) inflated the count further.

You have three levers, and they stack:

1. **Fixed monostable** (just committed) — now one pulse per rising edge, so the stutter/glitches near each note collapse into a single clean pulse. This alone should pull mono precision *above* raw instead of below.
2. **Higher strum threshold** — recall has huge headroom (~0.99), so raising the decision threshold cuts the liberal assertions cheaply, no retraining.
3. **Lower `pos_weight`** — the root fix; train less aggressively so the raw output isn't over-eager.

Run all three together:

```sh
cd tools/edge-ai
uv run edge-ai train --overfit ../marvin-perf/captures/slowride-hard-detfb.csv \
    --channels 64 --epochs 60 --tol 15 --window 96 \
    --strum-hold 8 --strum-refractory 4 --strum-thresh 0.7 --strum-weight 6
```

**What to look for now:**

## Where detfb's strum comes from

In `detector-fb`, the two label groups have **different sources**:
- **frets** ← detector `pressed_mask` (y=311, clean per-note structure, but ~220 ms *early* — releases before the strum)
- **strum** ← the in-frame `applied_mask` — the fretboard's **actual strum actuation**, correctly timed (~200 ms after the photo dip, same causal lag we measured)

So the **strum bit in detfb is identical to the one in actuator-fb** — it's the real strum, correctly timed. It is *not* wrong or inconsistent. And our strum eval (`strum_event_timing`) scores the strum bit in isolation, so the fret labels don't corrupt the strum numbers. The recall ~0.99 confirms strum is perfectly learnable here.

## So are we chasing a phantom? No — but you're half right

The over-firing is **not a dataset artifact** — it's the **training objective**: `pos_weight=17.3` makes the loss punish a missed strum 17× harder than a false one, so the model over-asserts. That's dataset-independent. The threshold / monostable / lower-weight levers all attack that, and they'll **transfer** to any dataset. So the strum tooling isn't wasted.

**Where your instinct is dead-on:** detfb is a **Frankenstein for *joint* training** — frets timed at y=311, strum timed at the strike line, ~220 ms apart, sharing one conv trunk. That's incoherent: the trunk gets pulled toward two different timings. It was built for exactly one job — proving the fret-structure hypothesis (done: frets → 0.99) — and you'd never deploy it (frets release before the strum). So we should **not finalize or over-tune on detfb.**

We've now extracted everything detfb can teach us:
- Clean fret *structure* → 0.99 frets ✓

The missing piece is a **single consistent dataset** where frets *and* strum are both clean and at strike-line timing. That's exactly what the **marvin line-263 change** produces: the actuator output releases frets between separate notes (clean structure) at the correct +220 ms timing, with the strum already correct. Then `actuator-fb` gives us coherent joint labels, and we tune frets + strum together on real data.

Hold for the test data — but yes, I really like that architecture, and it's the *right* place to put legato. Let me give you the honest assessment, including one gotcha that determines whether it works.

## The separation is correct

You're splitting two concerns that we'd been conflating:
- **What note is needed now** → the model/command layer. Clean, per-note, released between notes. Easy to learn, easy to distill.
- **How to physically drive it efficiently/reliably** → the fretboard actuator layer. Lazy hold to avoid release-repress thrash on fast same-fret runs.

That's exactly where legato belongs — a hardware-execution optimization, not something baked into the supervision. And the fretboard can do it **reactively, with no lookahead** (it doesn't have marvin's note queue): hold a fret until a *different* fret command arrives or a timeout fires. marvin's old suppression needed the queue; your version doesn't.

## The gotcha that makes-or-breaks it: what gets logged as the label

This is the part to get right. The training label currently is the fretboard's **`applied_mask` = the physical GPIO state** (`current_mask`). If you make the actuator lazy, then `applied_mask` *becomes the legato-held state again* — and we'd be logging exactly the polluted labels we just spent all this effort removing. We'd be back to square one without noticing.

So the label must be the **clean command the fretboard received**, *not* the lazy-held physical state. Two ways:
- **(a) Capture with lazy OFF.** Lazy is a play-mode feature; during training capture, apply marvin's clean per-note command directly so `applied_mask` == command == clean. Simplest.
- **(b) Log the received command separately.** Add a `commanded_mask` to the frame (the byte received, pre-lazy) and use *that* as the label; `applied_mask` stays the physical state for diagnostics.

I'd lean (a) for now — one less wire-format change, and lazy genuinely is a runtime-only concern.

## The lazy rule, and the one correctness constraint

Sketch: each fret, once asserted, stays down; it releases only when **a command arrives with a *non-empty, different* fret set that excludes it**, or after a **no-activity timeout**. Critically — **ignore the all-zero "gap" commands** (don't release on them); that's what gives you the lazy hold across same-fret gaps.

The correctness constraint: a **stale fret must be released before strumming a different chord**, or you'd play green+red when only red is wanted. That's satisfied as long as the model emits the *full correct fret set* for each note (which clean per-note labels do) — the fretboard diffs the new set and drops what's not in it, just before that note's strum.

## Sequencing

The **line-263 change is the real unblock** — it's needed for a clean dataset *regardless* of whether we ever build the lazy layer, and everything downstream depends on it. The **lazy actuator is a deferrable play-time optimization**, and mainly an *Expert-speed / slow-actuator* hedge: on hard mode (slow scroll) you likely have time to release+repress cleanly, and the actuator hardware is still TBD — so I wouldn't build it speculatively. Do line-263 → clean dataset → train; add lazy only if/when physical release-repress proves too slow on real hardware.

So: line-263 first (I'll implement when you give the word), capture with lazy off, and keep the lazy-actuator idea on the shelf for Expert. Let's see the strum sweep numbers when they land — if the fixed monostable + threshold recovered precision, that plus clean line-263 frets is a very promising hard-mode model.

Strong call, and the sustain point is the clincher — let me confirm the reasoning and then pin down *when* each piece is needed, because there's a timing nuance that simplifies the immediate step.

## Agreed on (b) — and here's exactly why it's required

Once the **lazy actuator exists, the physical state ≠ the command** (the fret stays down across gaps), so logging the physical `applied_mask` would re-pollute the labels. The label has to be the **commanded** byte. You're right, and (a) "capture with lazy off" would mean training in a different regime than you deploy — which, per your sustain point, is exactly what we can't afford.

## The sustain reasoning is correct — and the design already protects it

A sustain is held by **continuous detector `pressed`** (the gem tail occupies the row), which produces **no release edge** — so the line-263 suppression never fires on it. Releasing-between-notes touches only genuine note boundaries (release-edge + future need); **sustains stay commanded-held**. So we won't drop a sustain and trigger the "bar disappears" failure. And that failure mode is exactly why capture must happen in the **real play regime**: the robot's actuation feeds back through the controller → screen → photosensors, so a mishandled sustain would corrupt the very ADC stream we're learning from. Capturing in the deployed regime + logging the command is the consistent setup.

## The nuance: you get (b) for free *right now*, and it becomes load-bearing with lazy

Today there's **no lazy layer**, so the fretboard applies the command directly — `applied_mask` *already equals* the received command. So with just the **line-263 change**, the current `actuator-fb` labels are already the clean commanded byte. The *distinct* `commanded_mask` field only becomes necessary the moment lazy makes physical ≠ command. They're coupled — so ship `commanded_mask` **with** the lazy actuator, not before.

That gives a clean two-step that gets hard mode validated immediately and avoids a speculative wire break:

**Step 1 — now (hard mode + clean dataset):**
- marvin line-263: command released-style (release between separate notes; sustains held).
- Reflash **marvin only**, fretboard + wire unchanged. `applied_mask` == clean command.
- Re-capture slowride-hard → export `actuator-fb` → train. Expect ~0.99 frets *and* the strum we've been shaping, on one consistent dataset.

**Step 2 — Expert phase (coupled wire change, schema v5):**
- fretboard lazy actuation + add `commanded_mask` to the frame/record (the reserved byte absorbs it — record stays 32 B; frame 17→18 B).
- Exporter's `actuator-fb` switches its label source to `commanded_mask`.
- Re-capture Expert with lazy on; labels stay clean because we log the command, not the held state.

So you do get (b) — it lands with lazy, where it's needed — and we don't break the wire twice.

```text
1	"""Baseline causal 1D-CNN: 5 ADC channels over a window → 6 logits.
2	
3	Two dilated causal conv layers (so the receptive field spans the window with
4	few parameters), then a linear head on the last timestep. Output is 6 logits
5	(5 frets + collapsed strum) for independent weighted-BCE. int8 quantisation is
6	a Phase-3 concern; this trains in float32.
7	
8	Imports torch — only loaded when training/eval actually run.
9	"""
10	
11	from __future__ import annotations
12	
13	import torch
14	import torch.nn as nn
15	
16	from . import FRET_COUNT, N_LABELS
17	
18	
19	class CausalConv1d(nn.Module):
20	    """Conv1d with left padding only, so output[t] depends on inputs ≤ t."""
21	
22	    def __init__(self, in_ch: int, out_ch: int, kernel: int, dilation: int):
23	        super().__init__()
24	        self.pad = (kernel - 1) * dilation
25	        self.conv = nn.Conv1d(in_ch, out_ch, kernel, dilation=dilation)
26	
27	    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
28	        x = nn.functional.pad(x, (self.pad, 0))
29	        return self.conv(x)
30	
31	
32	class StrumNet(nn.Module):
33	    def __init__(
34	        self,
35	        *,
36	        channels: int = 8,
37	        kernel: int = 5,
38	        dilations: tuple[int, ...] = (1, 4),
39	        n_in: int = FRET_COUNT,
40	        n_out: int = N_LABELS,
41	    ):
42	        super().__init__()
43	        layers: list[nn.Module] = []
44	        prev = n_in
45	        for d in dilations:
46	            layers.append(CausalConv1d(prev, channels, kernel, d))
47	            layers.append(nn.ReLU())
48	            prev = channels
49	        self.features = nn.Sequential(*layers)
50	        self.head = nn.Linear(channels, n_out)
51	
52	    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
53	        # x: (B, n_in, window) -> features (B, channels, window) -> last step
54	        h = self.features(x)
55	        last = h[:, :, -1]
56	        return self.head(last)
57	
58	    @torch.no_grad()
59	    def predict_bits(self, x: torch.Tensor, thresh: float = 0.5) -> torch.Tensor:
60	        return (torch.sigmoid(self.forward(x)) >= thresh).int()
61	
62	
63	def count_macs(model: StrumNet, window: int) -> int:
64	    """Rough MAC count for one inference, to check against the on-device budget."""
65	    macs = 0
66	    for m in model.modules():
67	        if isinstance(m, nn.Conv1d):
68	            k = m.kernel_size[0]
69	            macs += m.in_channels * m.out_channels * k * window
70	        elif isinstance(m, nn.Linear):
71	            macs += m.in_features * m.out_features
72	    return macs
73
```

# model — StrumNet (the actual network)

What the model *is*, layer by layer, with the numbers that matter. Code: [`edge_ai/model.py`](../edge_ai/model.py). For the data it consumes see [`training.md`](training.md); for why we chose a CNN over MPLAB ML see the [journal](journal.md) decision log.

> **TL;DR.** A tiny causal 1D-CNN: 5 ADC channels → 2 dilated conv layers → a linear head on the **last timestep** → 6 sigmoids (5 frets + 1 strum). ~590 params at the default width. Two facts dominate everything: its **receptive field is only 21 samples (~88 ms)**, and the **deploy cost is far below what `count_macs` prints**.

---

## 1. Input

- **Shape:** `(batch, 5, window)` — 5 phototransistor ADC channels (G/R/Y/B/O), `window` consecutive 240 Hz samples, channels-first for `Conv1d`.
- **Normalisation:** per-channel standardise (zero-mean/unit-var) using stats computed on the training set and saved in the checkpoint ([`data.compute_norm_stats`](../edge_ai/data.py)). Deploy folds this into the int8 input affine.
- **Windowing:** sliced **by row index** within a contiguous `fb_seq` run, never by the bursty `timestamp` (see [journal](journal.md)).
- **At deploy:** one inference per 240 Hz tick, the window being the most recent `window` ADC samples.

## 2. Output

- **6 logits → sigmoids**, thresholded to bits: `[green, red, yellow, blue, orange, strum]`.
- Independent per-bit (no chord-shape coupling). Strum is the collapsed down|up bit; at the wire it maps to bit 5 (strum-down).
- Frets thresholded at 0.5; **strum has its own threshold** (`--strum-thresh`, default 0.5) because its recall has headroom and we trade it for precision. After thresholding, strum goes through the **monostable** post-processor ([`metrics.monostable`](../edge_ai/metrics.py)) — not part of the network.

## 3. Architecture, layer by layer

Default `StrumNet(channels=8, kernel=5, dilations=(1,4))`:

| Layer | Op | Out shape | Params |
|---|---|---|---|
| input | — | (5, W) | — |
| `CausalConv1d` 1 | Conv1d(5→8, k=5, **d=1**) + left-pad 4 | (8, W) | 5·8·5 + 8 = **208** |
| ReLU | — | (8, W) | — |
| `CausalConv1d` 2 | Conv1d(8→8, k=5, **d=4**) + left-pad 16 | (8, W) | 8·8·5 + 8 = **328** |
| ReLU | — | (8, W) | — |
| take last timestep | `h[:, :, -1]` | (8,) | — |
| `head` | Linear(8→6) | (6,) | 8·6 + 6 = **54** |
| | | **total** | **590** |

At `channels=64` (the diagnostic runs) it's **~22.6 k params** — RF and depth are unchanged, only width.

### Causal convolution
[`CausalConv1d`](../edge_ai/model.py) left-pads the input by `(kernel-1)·dilation` and uses a normal `Conv1d`, so `output[t]` depends only on inputs `≤ t` — no future leakage. That's what lets us train on whole windows and deploy as a streaming "predict-now" model.

## 4. Receptive field — the thing to internalise

Only the **last timestep** feeds the head (`h[:, :, -1]`). Its receptive field is:

\```
RF = 1 + Σ (kernel-1)·dilation = 1 + (5-1)·1 + (5-1)·4 = 21 samples ≈ 87.5 ms
\```

So the prediction at "now" depends **only on the last 21 ADC samples**, regardless of `channels`, and **regardless of `--window`**. Three consequences, all of which we've already seen:

1. **Widening the window does nothing.** Inputs older than 21 samples are convolved but never reach the head. This is exactly why `--window 96` and `128` gave no improvement over `60` — anything past ~21 is discarded.
2. **RF (21) < the photo→strum lag (≈48 samples / 200 ms on hard).** The causal photo dip that *causes* a strum sits ~48 samples back — **outside the receptive field.** The model can't see the dip directly. It works on hard mode only because slow scrolling makes each note's sensor occlusion *wide* enough that its tail reaches into the last 21 samples. Faster difficulties → narrower occlusion → less of it inside the RF → harder. This is a second, independent reason Expert was worse.
3. **The detector-fb fret result was flattered by timing.** detector-`pressed` (y=311) sits ~coincident with the photo dip (~5 samples apart), *inside* the RF — so frets hit 0.99 easily. **But `actuator-fb` frets are at strike-line timing (~48 samples after the dip), outside the RF.** Expect frets on the correctly-timed line-263 dataset to be **harder than the detfb 0.99**, limited by the same RF wall as strum — not because the structure is wrong, but because the network can't reach back to the cue.

**Fix direction (not yet done):** enlarge the RF to cover the lag — e.g. dilations `(1, 4, 16)` → RF = 1+4+16+64 = **85 samples (~354 ms)**, or a third layer, or replace the last-timestep head with temporal pooling over the window. This is the most likely next architecture change once we're on the consistent dataset.

## 5. Compute cost — `count_macs` is a loose upper bound

[`count_macs`](../edge_ai/model.py) multiplies conv cost by the **full window** (it assumes every output position is computed, as in dense training):

| config | `count_macs` (dense, ×window) |
|---|---|
| 8 ch, window 60 | ~31 k |
| 8 ch, window 96 | ~50 k |
| 64 ch, window 96 | ~2.12 M |

But at deploy you only need the **last timestep**, whose RF is 21 samples — so you compute a handful of conv positions, not the whole window:

| config | minimal deploy MACs (last timestep only) |
|---|---|
| 8 ch | conv1: 5 positions·200 + conv2: 1·320 + head 48 ≈ **1.4 k** |
| 64 ch | 5·1600 + 1·20480 + 384 ≈ **29 k** |

So against the ~100 k MAC/tick budget at 24 MHz, **even the 64-channel model fits comfortably** if deployed last-timestep-only (or incrementally, caching conv1 activations in a ring buffer). The "13× over budget" we kept saying is a `count_macs` artifact of the dense formula — real deploy cost is 1–2 orders of magnitude lower. **We are not as capacity-constrained as the printout implies** — relevant when we consider widening or deepening for the RF fix.

## 6. Training

- **Loss:** `BCEWithLogitsLoss` with a `pos_weight` vector — 1.0 on each fret, `pos_weight` on strum (auto = inverse strum frequency, ~10–17; override with `--strum-weight`). Strum sparsity (~5–9%) otherwise collapses it to "always 0". ([`train.train`](../edge_ai/train.py))
- **Optimiser:** Adam, lr 1e-3, batch 256.
- **Strum label dilation** (`--strum-dilate`): optionally widen the strum positive by ±k samples in the *training* labels so a near-miss isn't fully penalised (eval is never dilated).
- **Checkpoint** stores `state_dict`, `window`, `channels`, `kernel`, and the norm `mean`/`std`.

## 7. Inference & deployment

- **Threshold** the 6 sigmoids (frets 0.5, strum `--strum-thresh`).
- **Monostable** on the strum bit: rising-edge-triggered one-shot (`hold` ticks high, then `refractory` block) — guarantees clean uniform pulses, absorbs glitches, one strum per rising edge. A small counter; MCU-runtime friendly. ([`metrics.monostable`](../edge_ai/metrics.py))
- **Quantisation (Phase 3, not done):** int8 weights / int16 conv activations / int8 output; the target M0+ has no FPU so float inference is out. Standardisation + threshold fold into the input/output affines.

## 8. Known limitations / open design questions

- **Receptive field too small for the lag** (§4) — the headline issue. Almost certainly needs more dilation/depth or a pooling head before the correctly-timed `actuator-fb` frets and the strum can hit the gate robustly.
- **Last-timestep head discards the window** — a temporal pool (avg/max/attention over time) would actually *use* the window we feed and naturally widen the effective context.
- **Per-bit independence** — chords occupy a tiny subset of 2⁶; a chord-shape head or the two-head event detector ([review.md](review.md)) is the fallback if independence caps accuracy.
- **Capacity vs width** — 8 ch underfits strum recall, 64 ch fits well and (per §5) likely deploys fine; the right width is an open sweep, no longer obviously budget-bound.
- **No quantisation-aware training yet** — int8 effects on the tiny conv are unmeasured.

## What it documents

`StrumNet` end-to-end: input shape/normalization, the 6-sigmoid output, a layer-by-layer table (causal conv ×2 with dilations (1,4), last-timestep linear head, **590 params** at 8ch), the causal-padding mechanism, training loss/optimizer, and the deploy path (threshold → monostable → int8).

## Two things that surfaced while reading the code — and they matter now

**1. The receptive field is only 21 samples (~88 ms).** The head reads just the last conv timestep, whose RF is `1 + (5-1)·1 + (5-1)·4 = 21`. This single fact explains a lot:
- **Why widening `--window` did nothing** — anything older than 21 samples is convolved but never reaches the head.
- **Why Expert is harder** — the photo→strum lag is ~48 samples (200 ms), *outside* the 21-sample RF. The model can't see the causal dip directly; on hard mode it gets by only because slow scrolling makes each note's sensor occlusion wide enough that its *tail* lands inside the RF.
- **A heads-up for your next experiment:** the detfb 0.99 frets were flattered — detector-`pressed` sits ~coincident with the photo dip (inside the RF). But **`actuator-fb` frets are at strike-line timing, ~48 samples after the dip — outside the RF.** So when you run the line-263 `actuator-fb` overfit, don't be surprised if frets come out *below* 0.99; that wouldn't mean the structure regressed, it'd mean the network can't reach back to the cue. The fix is a bigger RF (dilations `(1,4,16)` → RF 85, or a pooling head).

**2. `count_macs` is a big overcount.** It multiplies by the full window (dense training cost). At deploy you only compute the last timestep (RF-worth): **~1.4k MACs at 8ch, ~29k at 64ch** — both well under the ~100k/tick budget. So the "64ch is 13× over budget" we kept repeating is an artifact; **we're not really capacity-constrained**, which matters because the RF fix likely means a slightly bigger net.

Net: the model is sound but its receptive field is the real bottleneck for correctly-timed labels — worth knowing before the next run so the numbers don't mislead. All uncommitted; tell me if/when you want it committed.

On the model: honestly there's **one real correction**, and it's the receptive field — the rest of what I listed is "could be better," not "wrong." Let me separate them.

## The one that matters: receptive field is undersized

RF = 21 samples (~88 ms), but the photo→strum lag is ~48 samples (~200 ms). The cue that drives the prediction sits *outside* what the head can see. That's not a bug — the net trains and runs fine — but it's the wrong size for the task, and it's been masked twice (window-widening did nothing; detfb's frets sat coincident with the cue). On correctly-timed `actuator-fb` data it'll bite.

**Fix:** add one dilated layer → `dilations=(1, 4, 16)` → RF = 1 + 4·(1+4+16) = **85 samples (~354 ms)**, covering the lag with margin. Keep the **last-timestep head**.

One correction to my *own* doc: I listed "a pooling head" as an alternative — I'd walk that back. For a precise predict-*now* task (especially strum onset), pooling over the window would blur *when*; widening the RF with dilations while keeping the last-timestep head is the right move. I'll fix that line in model.md.

And because deploy MACs are tiny (last-timestep only), the extra layer is essentially free on-device (~a few k MACs) — we're not budget-bound.

## The "could be better" (not corrections, don't touch yet)

- **Last-timestep head** — fine as-is once the RF is right.
- **Per-bit independence** — only revisit if chord structure caps accuracy (the two-head fallback in review.md).
- **Width (8 vs 64)** — an open sweep, no longer budget-limited; settle it on real data.
- **`count_macs`** — not wrong, just a loose (dense) upper bound; I could make it also print the last-timestep deploy cost. Cosmetic.

## How I'd validate (important: on the *right* data)

The RF only bites on correctly-timed labels, so the test has to be on the **line-263 `actuator-fb`** capture, not detfb. Cleanest: make `dilations` a CLI flag (default unchanged) so you can A/B **`(1,4)` vs `(1,4,16)`** on the same recapture and see whether the wider RF lifts frets/strum. That isolates the RF effect with no code churn between runs.

So sequencing stays: reflash marvin (line-263) → recapture → export `actuator-fb` → overfit with both dilation configs.

Want me to (a) fix the pooling line in model.md, and (b) add the `--dilations` flag now so it's ready for the A/B when you recapture? Both are small; I'll ask before committing either.
